keptItems.title: A Very Bad 24 Hours for Crypto
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk. Sign up here. Last night, hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange. The whole thing reportedly took about 20 minutes. It was the biggest theft in the history of the sector, and also probably the biggest financial heist of all time, topping the $1.5 billion ByBit hack of 2025 and Sadam Hussein’s $1 billion robbery of the Central Bank of Iraq in 2003. Binance says that about half of the stolen funds have been “frozen”—meaning that they’re effectively banned from being used in future transactions. North Korean hackers are thought to have been responsible. In the hours before the attack, though, a smaller heist was roiling a different corner of digital finance: Yesterday afternoon, at least $2.6 million was reportedly drained from Polymarket accounts. This, too, was a crypto theft. Polymarket’s international platform, which until last month hosted the majority of the company’s trading volume, runs on blockchain technology. But the attacks had different origins, and there’s no evidence that the two are connected. Binance is saying that its hack may have involved a compromised laptop, as well as “additional points of breach”; thieves took money that was stored on the exchange. On Polymarket, hackers exploited a flaw in a third-party provider, allowing them to access users’ accounts. It was the firm’s second security lapse since June. keptItems.title: The State Department Is in Disarray
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Many a heavy-handed metaphor has been constructed on the claim that Washington, D.C., is built on a swamp. This hoary cliché is also, for the most part, untrue —but the neighborhood Foggy Bottom, home to the State Department, really is former marshland . This is perhaps fitting. Stories of decadence, deviousness, and ineptitude within the current Trump administration are a dime a dozen, even at current inflation rates . The Justice Department acts as a private law firm for the president; the Department of Health and Human Services seems dedicated to undermining both; the Hegseth Pentagon is breaking globes, both physically and metaphorically . Yet the State Department has escaped some of the taint that has attached to other departments and agencies. This may be because the exploits elsewhere are so blatant, and because Secretary of State Marco Rubio has a reputation as one of the more serious figures in the administration. Whatever the reasons, the State Department may deserve more opprobrium than it has received. manifest.title: A Very Bad 24 Hours for Crypto
manifest.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk. Sign up here. Last night, hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange. The whole thing reportedly took about 20 minutes. It was the biggest theft in the history of the sector, and also probably the biggest financial heist of all time, topping the $1.5 billion ByBit hack of 2025 and Sadam Hussein’s $1 billion robbery of the Central Bank of Iraq in 2003. Binance says that about half of the stolen funds have been “frozen”—meaning that they’re effectively banned from being used in future transactions. North Korean hackers are thought to have been responsible. In the hours before the attack, though, a smaller heist was roiling a different corner of digital finance: Yesterday afternoon, at least $2.6 million was reportedly drained from Polymarket accounts. This, too, was a crypto theft. Polymarket’s international platform, which until last month hosted the majority of the company’s trading volume, runs on blockchain technology. But the attacks had different origins, and there’s no evidence that the two are connected. Binance is saying that its hack may have involved a compromised laptop, as well as “additional points of breach”; thieves took money that was stored on the exchange. On Polymarket, hackers exploited a flaw in a third-party provider, allowing them to access users’ accounts. It was the firm’s second security lapse since June.
